html:
The story takes place in the summer of 1998, in July. Two young men from Shandong, one 21 and one 22, leave their hometown for Beijing to find work.

In 1998 I was ten years old, in third grade at a primary school in a county town in Northeast China. I had been far from home only once, to the provincial capital.

Lately I’ve been hooked on the films of Huang Bo, one of China’s best-loved actors. I love his performances: they look almost like no acting at all, as if he were simply being himself, when in fact the acting is off the charts. It goes straight to your heart and makes you think. A while ago I watched Cow, the film that won him the Golden Horse Award for best actor, and he fully deserved every bit of that title. Get in, and Go was the first film of his life. It’s rough around the edges, but it’s still good, and it deserves more attention.

Back to the film itself. It is full of the feel and the marks of its era. In the twenty years since, some of them have long disappeared and some are still with us. The film lays out Chinese society at the turn of the century in full: buses whose maker you can’t make out, conductors hollering at the door and charging whatever they feel like, the old police uniforms and banknotes of the previous generation, bicycles far outnumbering cars, women’s glittering eye shadow, and what I thought only a big city like Beijing had back then: bars, with long-haired resident singers strumming songs by Jonathan Lee, the Taiwanese singer-songwriter.

And then the things that are still around today: people from the provinces coming to the capital to work, swaggering market inspectors, regional prejudice, money worship, the whole nation learning English, and Beijing’s bare-chested men who strip to the waist every summer.

The story is utterly true to life. Outsiders get pushed around by locals, business is hard going, love is impossible when the families aren’t a match, and those who do fall in love break up because they want different things. So the ones who still want to make it stay in Beijing, and the ones who are worn out go home to marry and have kids. The actors don’t ham it up with flailing arms; there’s no heart-rending screaming and glaring, no 360-degree spins of over-the-top coolness, and certainly no gorgeous idols with fancy double surnames racking up web traffic. There wasn’t much web traffic to be had back then. And only when you can’t tell whether you are watching acting or something that really happened does resonance arise on its own. It maps onto the path of your own life and sets you thinking. That, I think, is what film, poetry, music and the rest of art, those crystallizations of human wisdom, are meant to convey.

I went to university in 2007. It was in the provincial capital, not far from home, but that August was when I really left home and stopped living with my parents (an important yardstick for judging a person, East or West). That was 11 years ago. After six years of bachelor’s and master’s, in 2013 I came to Europe, 8,000 kilometers away. How different is a Chinese person in Europe from a Shandong man in Beijing? The language barrier, different cultural habits, locals who are sometimes, if not so obviously, against outsiders, clashing outlooks on life and values. Used to the Chinese rule of the road, “one, barge in; two, be sneaky; three, be fast,” whether crossing on foot or driving, I would end up in a standoff with drivers at intersections when I first came to Europe, because neither of us dared to go. When I went to Hong Kong with a German colleague, he was dejected for the first two days because he thought he must have done something wrong: why else would the waiters be so impatient, toss the menus onto the table and never make eye contact? There was also my first week in Europe, when a bunch of teenagers started yelling around me in the street. I chose not to notice and walked off quickly, because I was new in town and had no idea what they were up to. And then a while ago, another bunch of teenagers made slant-eye gestures at me, and I calmly said “f u” and gave them the middle finger. In my five years in Europe, many friends have gone back to China, while others stayed or moved on to other countries, just as Huang Bo goes back home to Shandong while his co-star Gao Hu holds on in Beijing. Stay abroad, and life and relationships are simple and low-key, the pace is slow, and you can trust the air and the food; the price is distance from your mother culture, from family and friends, plus the time and effort of learning the language and, more importantly, of integrating. Go back to China, and the opportunities and challenges in the market grow exponentially, you swim like a fish in the water of your mother culture, and although life is high-pressure, your fun and leisure can be absolutely rich and colorful.

I’m not tired of life abroad, and for now I have no plans to go back to China. Leaving academia wasn’t a whim, either. I decided after five years of continual shallow thinking, nearly six months of deep thinking and more than a month of concentrated thinking. It wasn’t an easy decision: it means a complete change of lifestyle, stepping out of my comfort zone, building something from nothing. But I don’t regret it, and I’m sure I won’t regret it in the future. In the whole process from resigning to finding a job, the only thing that sat badly with me was the guilt I felt toward my current boss. If turning him down five years ago, when I had to choose between two PhD offers, was still fair enough, then this time I signed his contract, kept on cleaning up after my PhD thesis on his time, and walked out the moment I graduated. That I can’t quite let go of yet. Here we go again: when I talked it over with European colleagues and friends, they generally found it perfectly normal and understandable, good for both parties, nothing to feel guilty about, whereas most of my Chinese friends knew exactly how I felt and understood my guilt. Cultural differences mean the same situation can strike entirely different chords. I once tried to explain against the backdrop of history, from the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods to the Opium Wars, the Cultural Revolution and reform and opening up, why Chinese people seem this way or that to Europeans. They said they finally understood more, but I’m sure their hearts didn’t resonate, just as some Europeans were convinced that the Chinese tourists recently thrown out of a hotel in Sweden must have been actors putting on a show. We grew up in different worlds, and cultural exchange is not as simple as learning the language.

I’ve just had an email from my current boss. In short, he was shocked, but after thinking it over he understands. He signed my resignation, dealt with a few handover matters, and even suggested we go for a drink before I officially leave. The nicer he is, the more shame on me. Maybe, looking back over our whole careers, this is no big deal; it’s just that the respect he has shown in handling the whole thing earns my admiration. Thinking about it rationally, my staying wouldn’t do either of us any good: one side with no motivation and no results, the other spending money and getting nothing back. It’s like the character Pigtail loving the high life in the nightclubs while Huang Bo wants to earn an honest living, or Gao Hu falling for the English teacher and thinking the feeling is mutual, when she just thinks he looks like her late younger brother.

So the line I’ll leave you with: whatever happens, the key is to make yourself happy.

Admit it: we are all selfish.
